inline.s: The temple keeps its spring-stones, iridescent as fine jade; / The seven patriarchs’ lamp returns to Eastern Yue; / Pitying the lingering soul, he ferries it across, / And brings it to the Land of Bliss, ending its long loss.
Submitted in homage by the eighty-one-year-old disciple Guifang.

In the Ming dynasty, it was in the Wanli era alone that there appeared, as manifested ancient Buddhas, three great elders: Master Lian, Master Da, and Master Han. Masters Lian and Da have no chronological biography; but having Master Han’s record of his eastern journey as their testament — a literary prajñā that illumined the earth and blazed in heaven, a hundredfold surpassing the spirit-transmission of Hutou (Gu Kaizhi) — it can in fact serve as the chronological biography of those two masters. As for Master Han, he wrote his own chronological biography at the time of his death-transformation, which was printed in Eastern Guangdong, but few ever saw it. My friend Tan Sao’an, as a student in his youth, early took refuge and received his name at the Master’s hands. The Master, at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci, had once on his own initiative entrusted his final affairs to him, that he might be a protector among kings and ministers. Later, when this biography was obtained, it was lost amid the war-fires of Guangdong. I (Wang Qilong), together with Shi Changwei, Shen Mingqi, and Gao Nianzu, came upon it at Dongchan, copied it by borrowing, and sent it south. By the time Sao’an returned home on leave, within a few days aboard his river boat, the commentary and readings had been completed. Examining in detail the records in the biography, and cross-checking them against what I myself had seen and what my ears had been taught — all the subtle esoteric explanations, the pointing off of heads, and those things that others could not have known — such as praying to protect the national root, reconciling the mother (Empress Dowager Cisheng) and the son (the Wanli Emperor), the plan to preach, like Dahui with his pot-cover, for certain years at the Land of the Untouchables in Leiyang, and his great Dharma-activities amid dangers, coming and going in Southern Yue — all this, the deportment of a great being, the manifestation of his very body, went beyond it. The brushwork of the biography resembles the Spring and Autumn Annals, while the statements and explanations of its beginnings and endings accord with the Zuozhuan (Commentary of Zuo). In the subtle words, beyond them, there are further disclosures; after the brush rested, he did not forget his charge of guardianship. In the Sacred Edition (Sheng bian), Sao’an could still verify and refine the chronological records of Confucius and Mencius as they passed through the Spring and Autumn and Warring States eras; how much more so for a master whom he attended morning and evening — and through whom he could requite the milk of the Dharma and benefit the students, as though the assembly on Vulture Peak had not yet dispersed? May those who see it think of it as a rarity, as a thing hard to encounter and hard to meet; and let them not say that, in the essential part wherein Caoxi was revived, this is still merely the second moon. The lay disciple of Xiushui, Wang Qilong, bathed and perfumed, respectfully writes this postscript.
Appendix: Three Dharma-talks from the Eastern Journey Collection
At the Jingshan Chan Hall: Instruction on the Essentials of Chan Practice

The Chan school is the transmission of the Buddha’s mind-seal, and is by no means a trivial matter. From the beginning, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he established the aim of the single transmission, sealing the mind with the four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra. So although Chan is a separate transmission outside the teachings, in truth it is verified by the teachings, and only then is the Buddha’s and the patriarchs’ way of non-duality seen. The work of investigation is likewise derived from the teachings. The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: reflecting in the mountain forest, in superior, middling, and inferior practice, one sees the thought-flow of delusion in one’s own mind — this is indeed the World-Honored One’s direct teaching of the essential method for doing the work. It also says: mind, thought, and consciousness are projections of one’s own mind; the realm of self-nature, the thoughts of delusion, the ocean of birth and death, karmic love and ignorance — these causes, one and all, are to be transcended; this is the Tathāgata’s direct showing of the wondrous purport of awakening the mind. It further says: from the sages above, transmitted from one to another, deluded thought is without self-nature — this, again, is his direct showing of the secret mind-seal. These are the crucial points the Yellow-faced Elder (the Buddha) taught for investigation and reflection. When Bodhidharma showed the second patriarch, he said: “Only put to rest all the conditions without, and make the mind within have no panting; let the mind be like a wall, and you may enter the Way.” This is the essential method Bodhidharma first taught people for investigation. When the transmission reached Huangmei (the Fifth Patriarch), who was seeking a Dharma-successor, the Sixth Patriarch had just said “Originally there is not a single thing,” and so received the robe and bowl — this is the direct purport of the transmitted mind-seal. When the Sixth Patriarch returned south, Huiming and others pursued him to Gengling to seize the robe and bowl; the Patriarch placed them on a rock, and Huiming could not lift them. Huiming said, “I have come for the Dharma.” The Patriarch said, “Since you have come for the Dharma, then only cast off all external conditions and let not even a single thought arise; then I shall speak for you.” Huiming was silent for a long time. The Patriarch said, “Without thinking of good, without thinking of evil, at just this very moment, what is Venerable Ming’s original face?” Huiming was instantly greatly enlightened. This is the Sixth Patriarch’s first direct instruction on the essential method of investigation. Thus we know that the Buddhas and patriarchs of old simply taught people to awaken to their own mind and recognize themselves; there had never been any talk of gong’an or huatou. As it went down to Nanyue and Qingyuan, the patriarchs gave instruction as suited the occasion, for the most part striking right at the point of doubt, making people turn back and, once their head turned, come to rest. Even among those who did not understand, though the tongs and hammer were applied, it was left only to the causes and conditions of the time. It was only with Huangbo that one began to be taught to look into a huatou. And it was not until Chan Master Dahui that one energetically urged students to investigate a gong’an of the ancients as a handle, calling it a huatou, and required them to lift it up intensely. Why? Because in the students’ field of the eighth consciousness, the evil-habit seeds from countless kalpas have been inwardly perfuming them thought after thought, continuing and flowing on, with delusion never ceasing, and there is nothing to be done about it. And so a single flavorless phrase is given for you to grip firmly: first set down together all the inner and outer, mind and object, considerations and delusions. Because you cannot put them down, you are taught to lift this huatou, like cutting a tangled thread — once cut, all is cut, and it does not continue. This cuts off the train of consciousness, and does not let it pass through again — this is precisely Bodhidharma’s rule of “put to rest the conditions without, the mind within without panting, the mind like a wall.” If you do not set to work this way, you will certainly never see your own original face. It is not that you are taught to ponder over the words of the gong’an, taking them as a doubt-mass, and hope to get a clear answer from it. Yet even so, Dahui exclusively taught the contemplation of the huatou and applied the deadly blade — only to make you kill the thieving mind. For he showed the assembly: “In Chan practice, only make the mind utterly empty; paste the two characters birth-and-death on your forehead, like one who owes a man ten thousand strings of cash. Three periods a day and three periods a night, amid tea and amid rice, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whether bantering with friends, whether quiet or busy, hold up a huatou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhaozhou said, ‘No.’ Just keep looking into it again and again. When there is no flavor, it is like striking against a wall. When you come to the end of the tangle, like a mouse entering a cow’s horn, then the collapse is seen. You must make up a long-enduring body and mind to wrestle with it. Suddenly the mind-flower bursts into bloom, illumining the temples of the ten directions — one awakening, and you are thoroughly done.” These are the tongs and hammer that Dahui, the old man, habitually used. His meaning is only this: make the huatou block the flowing delusion beneath the faculty of mind; and right where it does not flow, there look for the original face. It is not that he taught you to ponder the gong’an and, taking it as a doubt-mass, to seek a resolution. As he said, “The mind-flower bursting into bloom — how could it be obtained from another?” The Buddhas and patriarchs above, one after another, pointed this out: they require you to investigate yourself, not to go seeking from profound and mysterious phrases. Today, when people practice Chan and do the work, everyone says they look into a huatou and set up a doubt-mass; but they do not know to investigate at the root, and only seek on the surface of the huatou. Seeking again and again, suddenly they conjure up a scene out of imagination and say they are enlightened; then they produce a verse and present a eulogy, take it as a rare treasure, and think they have attained. Little do they know that they have wholly fallen into the net of delusion and intellectual views. Practicing Chan in this way — does it not blind the eyes of the whole world and of later generations? Young people of today, before the meditation-cushion is even settled, call themselves awakened to the Way, give free rein to their mouths, and play with their spirit, taking it for quick wit. They think out a few confused, unfounded words and call them eulogies on the ancients — but these come from their own delusion; have they ever, even in a dream, met the ancients? If people today could awaken to the Way so easily, then the bearing of the ancients — such as Changqing sitting through and wearing out seven meditation-cushions, and Zhaozhou not mixing his mind for forty years — set beside this, would make the ancients the dullest of faculties, not fit even to carry today’s straw sandals. Overweening persons, who have not attained yet claim attainment — is that not to be feared? In Chan practice, looking into the huatou and setting up the doubt-mass is absolutely indispensable — what is called ‘small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening; no doubt, no awakening.’ The point is only to use the doubt-mass well. Once the doubt-mass is broken, the nostrils of the Buddhas and patriarchs are naturally drawn through on a single string. For example, in the gong’an of Buddha-recitation, one only investigates who it is that recites the Buddha’s name; it is not a doubt about who the Buddha is. If you doubt who the Buddha is, you have only to hear the lecturer speak of Amitabha Buddha, whose name is Immeasurable Light, and take that as enlightenment, composing a few verses on Immeasurable Light. If that is called awakening to the Way, then those who awaken the mind would be as dense as hemp and as many as millet — how pitiable! The ancients spoke of the huatou as a tile for knocking at the door: it is only to knock open the door and see the person inside, not to busy oneself about work outside the door. From this it is clear that when one sets up doubt by means of the huatou, the doubt lies not in the huatou but at the root. Consider Jiashan calling on the Boat Monk (Chuansi): he asked, “A thousand feet of line is let down, the intent lies in the deep pool. Three inches from the hook, why does the gentleman not speak?” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the Master knocked him into the water with his oar. As soon as Jiashan climbed back on the boat, the Master again said, “Speak, speak.” As Jiashan was about to speak, the Master struck again. Jiashan was greatly awakened, and nodded three times. The Master said, “The line at the tip of the pole is yours to play with; without violating the blue waves, the intention is itself distinct.” If Jiashan had busied himself with the hook and line, how could the Boat Monk have risked his life for him? This is the ancients’ easy and well-turned path of liberation. In the past, when the Way of Chan flourished, there were clear-eyed knowing ones everywhere, and many in the world practiced investigation, with realization breaking forth wherever they went. Moreover it was said, “It is not that there is no Chan; it is only that there is no teacher.” Today the Chan school has been desolate for a long time. How fortunate that so many at a stroke have set their minds to investigate! Though there are knowing ones, some measure the faculties and advance them provisionally, and confirm according to their own feelings. The students’ minds being shallow, they take it for attainment; and, moreover, they do not trust the Buddha’s sage teachings, do not seek the true head of the road, and only muddle along — even taking the gourd-stamp (a forged seal) as the decisive guarantee. Not only do they wrong themselves, they also wrong others — is that not to be feared? For instance, among the officials and lay practitioners of old recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp, there were but a few. But among those who toil in worldly dust today, without cultivating even the gross precepts, with turbid and delusive thoughts, relying on their own cleverness, they read a few encounters of the ancient worthies and every one regards himself as of the highest faculty; meeting a monk, they vie with him in wit, and likewise take themselves to have awakened to the Way. Though this is a defect of the times, in truth it is because our own fellows — one blind man leading many blind men. I, the old man, would not dare to talk arrogantly beyond my station; now, following the true essentials of the Buddhas’ and patriarchs’ practice, I discuss it with one and all. The wise and lofty are naturally able to set it right.
At the Yunqi Abbot’s Quarters: Instruction on the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation

The gate of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is in the first place about the great matter of ending birth and death; hence it is said, “Recite the Buddha and end birth and death.” People today set their minds because they want to end birth and death, and only then are willing to recite the Buddha. If one merely says that reciting the Buddha can end birth and death, without knowing at what point the root-stock of birth and death is ultimately to be ended, then if the mind of recitation cannot sever the root-stock of birth and death, how can birth and death be ended? What is the root-stock of birth and death? The ancients said: “If karmic offenses were not heavy, one would not be born in the Sahā world; if love were not cut off, one would not be born in the Pure Land.” Thus we know that the root of love is the root-stock of birth and death. Because all sentient beings undergo the suffering of birth and death through the fault of love and desire. Tracing back this root of love, it is not something that exists in this life alone, nor in one, two, three, or four lives; rather, ever since the very beginning of birth and death in the beginningless past, life after life, giving up the body and receiving a body, it has all been the flow of love and desire — down to today. Looking back, was there ever a single thought momentarily apart from this root of love? A seed of the root of love, accumulated and deepened through kalpas, is why birth and death are endless. Today, just when one has begun to set the mind to recite, vainly hoping to be reborn in the West, one does not even know the very name that love is the root of birth and death — how could there have been a single thought of cutting it? Since one does not know the root of birth and death, then while reciting on the one hand, the root of birth and death is only left to grow; the recitation and birth and death have nothing to do with each other. Then, no matter how you recite, when you come to the end of your life, you will see the root of birth-and-death love manifesting before you; only then will you know that the recitation had no power, and you will blame the Buddha-recitation for having no efficacy — but the repentance is too late. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha today first to know that love is the fundamental root of birth and death, and that in reciting, thought after thought, one must sever this root of love. That is, in your daily life before you, reciting while at home, what your eyes see — sons, daughters, grandchildren, family, property — there is not one that is not an object of love; so there is not one thing, not one thought, that is not the livelihood of birth and death, just as if one were wholly in a pit of fire. Yet, unaware, at the very time of reciting, the root of love in the heart has not been let go of for a single thought. Just so, at the very time of reciting, one says only that the recitation is not intense, not knowing that love is the master and recitation only the surface: the Buddha is merely reciting, and love is merely growing. For instance, when affection for sons and daughters appears before you, turn the light back and see whether this single sound of the Buddha can indeed hold in check this love, indeed sever this love. If it cannot sever this love, then in the end how is birth and death to be ended? Because the conditions of love are practiced and familiar through many lives, while the recitation of the Buddha has only just begun to be aroused and is very unfamiliar and not earnest — therefore one obtains no power from it. If you cannot master the love-realm before you now, then at the end of life you certainly will not be able to master it. Therefore I urge the one who recites the Buddha: the first thing is to know the urgency of the heart for birth and death. To be urgent in ending birth and death, one must, at the root-stock of birth and death, cut off thought after thought; then each thought is the very moment of ending birth and death. Why must you wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month (the end of life) to settle it? That is the latest of the late. As it is said, all of what is before you is a matter of birth and death; if right before you birth and death are ended, then it is empty. If you make each thought true and real in this way, each stroke drawing blood, and with such a mind you do not escape birth and death, then the Buddhas all fall into false speech. Therefore, whether at home or having left home, only know the mind of birth and death — that is the very time to escape birth and death. Is there any other wonderful method beyond this?
At the Jingci Zongjing Hall: Instruction on Holding the Cundi Dharani, spoken for the disciples Tan Fuzheng and others

Lay practitioners dwelling at home have the five desires thick and the roots of affliction deep. Day by day the manifesting afflictions crisscross before them, like a seething cauldron rolling on — how could they gain so much as a single thought of coolness? Even if they set their mind to practice, it is hard for them to begin the work. Those who are clever and study the teachings only learn a few views to furnish their talk, with absolutely no practical use. As for reciting the Buddha, they take it as an ordinary thing and will not make an all-out resolve. Even if they would, they gain no power, because they recite only on the surface of drifting thoughts; in reality the hidden habit-currents flowing in the store consciousness are completely unseen, and so their recitation has never shown a single thought coming to rest. If recitation of the Buddha had power, how could one need to seek something else profound and mysterious? Now there is a kind who love the lofty and delight in the strange: hearing of investigating Chan and of sudden awakening, they take themselves to be of the highest faculties and will not cultivate, for fear of falling into gradual stages. On the encounters of the ancient worthies they memorize a few obliging phrases and blather on, seeking only quickness and ease as a display of wit; these are the most pitiable of all. In view of this, if one truly sets the mind in fear of birth and death, it is better to enter by way of holding the mantra — because one first brings a whole-hearted earnest mind, power is easily gained. The student Tan Fuzheng asked for the essentials of practicing while at home, and so I showed him this. Let those who look upon it not take it as unreasonable, for reason has misled people far too much. Therefore this gate is even more excellent than investigating the cypress tree, or the dry turd (two famous gong’an).
The Original Preface to the Eastern Journey Collection

Master Han, with a single breath, roamed through the whole Avataṃsaka cosmos; his words filled the lands past counting — the lands of ineffable number — and their harmony and elegance, so subtle and wondrous, make even the West cherish his fine sound; what need to ask about the East? Lord He and Scholar Liang gathered the four fascicles of the Eastern Journey — is this not what is meant by the broad and long tongue covering the Eastern world? When the Master went east to mourn Zibo at Shuangjing and to mourn Lianchi at Yunqi, compared with the four kindnesses it was a fine requital indeed. The two compositions raise the sun and moon to mid-heaven, and their threads also cover the seven mansions of the Azure Dragon. The people of the East, likening them to such casual jottings as the ‘Ru Tui’ (retreat), view them with the eyes of flesh, and wrongly name Zibo the fierce warrior, Lianchi the kind mother, and Han Shan the chivalrous king.

and so, dwelling amid the words of wisdom, he said: ‘Our Master! Our Master! Supposing he transformed his left foot into Lianchi’s thousand-spoked wheel treading in succession, and transformed his right foot into Zibo’s thousand-radiant wheels treading in measure — the twin feet of the Two Honored Ones have already appeared. The honored feet remain; alone he wanders the human world. Can one call this the poverty of Hou Kui? Soon he will return to rest at Yunqi; with feet bound, turning back the radiance, he complies with the request of our followers. Speaking of the East while in the East — can the ink of seas and the brush of forests suffice to record it? At the beginning the Master wandered and dwelt at Jianye, and together with Quhe and Xuelang pondered in the same way Zhuangzi, Laozi, and the Records of the Historian; gaining the wisdom of mutual response, he expounded the Śūraṅgama Sūtra until dawn, and shadows, echoes, snares, and fish-traps were all consigned to a single illusion. What the horizontal mouth set forth, what the horizontal hand set turning — like a channel drawing in a river and its current, a wheel flying and a gem revolving, suddenly with no pause of mechanism. Those rain-flowers at Yaoshan, the casual jottings of the ‘Ru Tui’ — why this cramped fussiness? Because, mourning the two Masters, he gained two outstanding disciples: Hegong of the You-Xia kind, and Scholar Liang of the An-Yuan kind — will they not well continue the sound? Yet the opportunity and the subtlety emerge together, the true and the worldly blend into one; cutting away the view of self, there is no Dharma to give to others. Our Master! Our Master! Truly it is hard to carry on. The people of the East ask: what, in the end, is it?’

In the Master’s Eastern Journey Collection, there are three great Dharma-talks that were conferred and bequeathed, together with the original preface of the great layman Yu Deyuan of Wulin; these I respectfully call out and append to the last leaves of the chronological biography, to show to all quarters, holding also lest one for an instant forget the occasion at Zongjing. The disciple Fuzheng respectfully makes this known.
